title: Explain why a plan is rejected

blocks.text: The planning tool rejects plans, and planners keep asking *why*. A rejection that only says "infeasible" sends them to the spreadsheet; one that names the broken rule lets them fix the plan in a minute.
Write `evaluate_plan(projects, budget, plan)` in `plans.py`. It returns a pair: the plan's total value, and a list of problems, one string for each rule the plan breaks:

rows: the plan's total cost is over `budget`
a must-do project is not in the plan (one string per missing project)
project `<id>` is in the plan and its parent is not
the plan holds more than one project of alternative group `<group>`

blocks.text: An allowed plan returns its value and an empty list. The order of the problems does not matter. `projects` is a list of `Project` records (defined at the top of the file) and `plan` is a set of project ids.

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Project:
    pid: str
    cost: int
    value: int
    must_do: bool = False
    parent: str | None = None
    group: str | None = None


def evaluate_plan(projects: list[Project], budget: int, plan: set[str]) -> tuple[int, list[str]]:
    """Return the plan's total value and one problem string per rule it breaks."""
    by_id = {p.pid: p for p in projects}
    chosen = [by_id[pid] for pid in plan]
    problems = []
    if sum(p.cost for p in chosen) > budget:
        problems.append("budget")
    problems += [f"must-do:{p.pid}" for p in projects if p.must_do and p.pid not in plan]
    problems += [f"parent:{p.pid}" for p in chosen if p.parent and p.parent not in plan]
    groups = [p.group for p in chosen if p.group]
    problems += [f"alternatives:{g}" for g in sorted(set(groups)) if groups.count(g) > 1]
    return sum(p.value for p in chosen), problems


if __name__ == "__main__":
    demo = [Project("A", 50, 80, must_do=True), Project("B", 30, 40), Project("C", 20, 35, parent="B")]
    print(evaluate_plan(demo, 90, {"A", "C"}))

cases.says: an allowed plan reports its total value and no problems
a plan that spends exactly the budget is within it
a must-do project's cost counts against the budget like any other
a plan missing one of two must-do projects is reported for the missing one
a parent project funded without its child is allowed
a child funded without its parent is reported, naming the child
funding no project of an alternative group is allowed
two projects from one alternative group are reported, naming the group

origin.section: Constraints Decide Which Plans Are Allowed, and Business Rules Are Constraints Too

concepts: a plan's objective is one number, the sum of the funded projects' values
must-do, parent-child and alternative rules restrict which plans are allowed, exactly as the budget does
